newsitem.title: USA: World buyers seen sticking to U.S. soy until March.
newsitem.headline: World buyers seen sticking to U.S. soy until March.

text.p: Tuesday's sharp rally in U.S. soybean futures did little to temper export demand, and analysts and traders said buyers would continue to buy U.S. supplies for at least two more weeks.

"The calendar will do as much to stop (demand) as price does," said Roy Huckabay, vice-president and analyst at LIT, a division of First Options. "By the time we get into early March we'll be into a lot of South American beans."
Taiwan and South Korea bought U.S. soybeans early Wednesday despite an 18-cent per bushel rally Tuesday.
Taiwan had passed on a tender for U.S. soybeans on Friday, citing high prices.
"They panicked," one Chicago Board of Trade floor trader said. "They saw the technical breakout yesterday and they thought we were going higher so they had to buy."

Analysts said buyers were still willing to pay a premium for U.S. supplies to guarantee early March shipment instead of waiting for South American soybeans in early April. They said buyers were also concerned that weather or logistical problems might delay shipment from Brazil and Argentina.

"From now until the end of March, you're going to have to go to the U.S.," said Joel Karlin, analyst with Everen Securities. "Nobody's very comfortable even with the fact that Brazil has a record crop."

Trade sources said Brazil's infrastructure and port system cannot handle the volume of grain that passes through U.S. ports and some buyers were hesitant to rely on a system not accustomed to shipping large quantities on tight schedules.
They also pointed to reports that unsettled weather in Brazil's Parana state could delay export shipments out of Paranagua port for months.

"They can't move the trainloads of grain to the ports and load it into vessels the way we can," another CBOT trader said. "If they have any logistical or weather problems, you'd better believe buyers will pay whatever the market demands."
The U.S. Agriculture Department forecast Brazil and Argentina would produce bumper crops, and their export prices for April shipment were already below U.S. values.
USDA in its February crop report estimated Brazil's soybean output at 26.5 million tonnes, up from its January estimate of 26.0 million tonnes. Brazil harvested 23.4 million tonnes last year.
Argentina's production was pegged at 13.5 million tonnes, up from USDA's January estimate of 13.0 million and above last year's production of 12.64 million.
But world demand was projected to devour the increased supply. The European Union alone was forecast to import more than Argentina's entire production.
By early March, when Brazil's harvest should be well under way, cheaper prices should outweigh logistical concerns and shift buyers' focus south, LIT's Huckabay said.

"You're already starting to see the basis in Brazil drop off to new crop levels," he said. "U.S. beans are 30 to 35 cents over Brazil for April. You're looking at difficulty in maintaining new sales out of the U.S." after March.
